== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:
   - If `Retrieval status` is `not_accessible` (or the paper text below says `[FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE]`), you MUST set `paper_read = "not accessible"`, `study_design_identified = "cannot_tell (full text not accessible)"`, `chosen_tool = "cannot_tell"`, `why_tool_chosen = "full text not accessible"`, `overall_rating = "cannot_tell"`, `domain_ratings = []`, all 7 `cross_tool_domains` fields to `"cannot_tell"`, `overall_narrative_summary = "Full text not accessible; no risk-of-bias appraisal performed."`, `where_found_summary = "not accessible"`, and `evidence_quotes = []`. NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / Moderate concern for item and survey nonresponse: No longitudinal follow-up applies, but overall survey response rate is unreported, 7 of 97 respondents (7.2%) are excluded from correlation/regression models (N = 90) without explicit missing-data accounting (potentially linked to an unexplained 'Hungarian subsample' restriction on p. 5), and only 30 of 97 respondents (30.9%) provided evaluable open-ended qualitative responses (p. 8).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: Gender comparisons on survey items (Welch's ANOVA, Table 2, p. 7) and observational restroom usage times (Section 3.3, p. 9) are completely unadjusted. Multiple linear regressions (N = 90, p. 7) adjust only for binary gender and coarse ordinal age brackets (plus an experience composite), omitting key confounders such as parental/caregiving status, disability or health needs, frequency of public-space travel, facility design, and peak internal queue congestion during time observations.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate doctrinal framing, not empirically operationalized: The article accurately identifies relevant EU/UN equality and sanitation instruments (Council Directive 2004/113/EC, EU Charter Art. 23, UNGA Res. 64/292 & 76/153, UN Special Rapporteur reports) and comparative building standards (Hungarian Gov. Reg. Nr. 280/2024, Singapore COPEH, Australian NCC Table F4D4, UK BS 6465 guidance, German ASR A4.1 and DIN 18040-1:2010-1; pp. 2-4, 10, 12-13), organizing them into a conceptual tripartite accountability matrix (Table 1, p. 4). However, legal standards are not coded or measured as empirical exposure variables in the survey or observational study.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Survey constructs rely on an unvalidated ad hoc questionnaire with sub-threshold internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.601; McDonald's omega = 0.640, p. 6), self-reported recall, and a direct Likert polarity contradiction between Table 2's footnote ('1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree', p. 7) and the main text ('lower scores indicate stronger agreement', pp. 6-7). Chronometric restroom observations (N = 56, pp. 5-6, 9) combine entry-to-exit time without separating internal waiting, fixture use, and handwashing, omit external queue time, lack inter-rater reliability protocols, and display discrepant means between Table 4 (~126 s men, ~159 s women) and the text (121.25 s men, 136.63 s women, p. 9).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Subjective outcomes (perceived safety, satisfaction, need for additional women's toilets, nappy-changing barriers) rely on single-item or low-reliability composite self-reports with inconsistent coding documentation (pp. 6-8). Objective restroom duration is measured in only one university building during a single 40-minute break (N = 56) without isolating waiting vs. fixture service time and without reporting variance (SD/IQR) or inferential statistical tests (pp. 5-6, 9-10).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern: No pre-registration or full survey instrument is provided. Section 3.1 selectively reports statistics only for the four survey items showing significant gender differences (Table 2, pp. 6-7) while omitting estimates for non-significant items; Hypothesis H4 is declared 'clearly support[ed]' using raw means alone with no inferential test (pp. 9-10); and Sections 4.1 and 4.5 repeatedly cite 'queuing simulations' (pp. 10, 15) whose methods, parameters, and results never appear in Methods or Findings.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Both empirical strands use convenience sampling with severe demographic and contextual skew. The survey (N = 97) recruited university students and unspecified social media users, yielding 72.2% women and 63.9% aged 18-29 (pp. 5-6, 14), with no sampling frame or response rate reported. The chronometric study observed N = 56 users during a single 40-minute midday interval at one university building in Gyor (p. 9), limiting generalizability to broader municipal public toilets or tourism settings discussed in the paper (pp. 4, 15).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S1: Are there clear research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: The Abstract, Introduction (pp. 1-5), and Methods section (p. 6) clearly articulate the exploratory empirical aims and state four explicit directional hypotheses (H1-H3 for the questionnaire survey on safety, women's toilet capacity, and dignity; H4 for the time-measurement study on gendered restroom use duration).
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Section 1 (PDF pp. 2, 5); Section 2 Methods (PDF p. 6)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: The combination of structured survey items (N = 97), open-ended narrative responses (n = 30), and chronometric restroom duration observations (N = 56) provides primary empirical data aligned with the exploratory research questions and hypotheses H1-H4, despite sampling and measurement limitations.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Methods (PDF pp. 5-6); Section 3 Findings (PDF pp. 6-10)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Qualitative thematic content analysis of users' open-ended accounts is appropriate for exploring subjective meanings, lived inconveniences, privacy and menstruation concerns, and caregiving barriers in public sanitation use.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Methods (PDF p. 5); Section 3.2 Qualitative Findings (PDF pp. 8-9)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.2: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Qualitative data come solely from optional open-ended items appended to a self-administered questionnaire, answered by 30 of 97 respondents (24 women, 6 men). Exact prompt wording, response length/depth, and whether thematic saturation was reached are not reported, leaving the adequacy of qualitative data collection uncertain.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Methods (PDF p. 5); Section 3.2 Qualitative Findings (PDF p. 8)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: Section 3.2 states that 'Thematic content analysis with multiple coding' was performed and organizes findings into two broad domains and five coded themes (Table 3), but provides no explanation of the coding protocol, number of coders, discrepancy resolution, reflexivity, or theme frequencies across the 30 respondents.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.2 Qualitative Findings and Table 3 (PDF pp. 8-9)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: Table 3 pairs each of the five qualitative themes (privacy breach, hygiene breakdown, forced commercial workaround, care burden, waiting/queues) with clear definitions and verbatim illustrative quotations attributed by gender and age bracket, substantiating the interpretive claims in Sections 3.2 and 4.2-4.3.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.2 and Table 3 (PDF pp. 8-9); Sections 4.2-4.3 (PDF pp. 11-13)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.5: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: There is logical alignment among the exploratory research aims on everyday sanitation barriers, the open-ended experience prompts, the five thematic categories in Table 3, and the normative-institutional interpretation regarding privacy, care work, and dignity.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 (PDF p. 5); Section 3.2 (PDF pp. 8-9); Sections 4.2-4.3 (PDF pp. 11-13)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.1: Is the sampling strategy relevant to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Recruitment relied on convenience distribution among university students supplemented by unspecified social media platforms, plus an unexplained reference to 'the Hungarian subsample' for attitudinal items (p. 5), while chronometric observations were restricted to a single university building break (p. 9). Because target population boundaries, eligibility criteria, and recruitment channels are insufficiently specified—and student-heavy campus sampling only loosely maps onto broader urban public-space and caregiving mobility—relevance of the sampling strategy cannot be confirmed.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Methods (PDF pp. 5-6); Section 3.1 (PDF p. 6); Section 3.3 (PDF p. 9)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.2: Is the sample representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: The survey sample (N = 97) is small and severely skewed toward women (72.2%, n = 70) and 18-29-year-olds (63.9%, n = 62), and the observational sample covers only 56 users during one 40-minute interval at Szechenyi Istvan University in Gyor. Section 4.5 explicitly acknowledges that the data come from 'a relatively small, nonrepresentative sample (N = 97), with a pronounced overrepresentation of women and younger respondents'.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.1 (PDF p. 6); Section 3.3 (PDF p. 9); Section 4.5 Limitations (PDF pp. 14-15)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.3: Are the measurements appropriate?
domain_ratings.justification: Measurements exhibit substantial validity and reliability flaws: (1) the ad hoc questionnaire scale falls below standard reliability thresholds (Cronbach's alpha = 0.601; McDonald's omega = 0.640, p. 6); (2) Table 2's footnote defines the need-for-women's-toilets Likert item as '1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree, with higher scores indicating stronger agreement', directly contradicting the text on pp. 6-7 stating that 'lower scores reflect stronger agreement'; (3) chronometric 'restroom use time' conflates internal waiting, cubicle/urinal use, and handwashing while excluding external queue waiting (pp. 5-6); and (4) Table 4 reports 'Own results, 2025' as ~126 s (men) and ~159 s (women), conflicting with the overall means reported in the text (121.25 s and 136.63 s, p. 9).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 (PDF pp. 5-6); Section 3.1 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 6-7); Section 3.3 and Table 4 (PDF p. 9)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.4: Is the risk of nonresponse bias low?
domain_ratings.justification: No information is provided on how many individuals were invited or exposed to the student/social-media questionnaire, precluding response-rate calculation or non-respondent analysis; furthermore, regression and correlation analyses drop from N = 97 to N = 90 (pp. 7-8) without explaining the missing 7 cases.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.5: Is the statistical analysis appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Although Welch's ANOVA and OLS regressions with collinearity checks are used for survey items, major analytical deficiencies remain: (1) Hypothesis H4 on restroom duration (N = 56, pp. 9-10) is judged 'clearly support[ed]' solely from raw means without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or any inferential statistical test; (2) multiple item-by-item gender tests are conducted without multiplicity correction and non-significant item statistics are omitted; (3) four-category ordinal age brackets are entered as continuous linear predictors/variables in OLS and cross-sectional mediation models (pp. 7-8); and (4) Sections 4.1 and 4.5 invoke 'queuing simulations' (pp. 10, 15) for which no mathematical specification or results are presented.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.1 (PDF pp. 6-8); Section 3.3 (PDF pp. 9-10); Sections 4.1 and 4.5 (PDF pp. 10, 15)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Sections 2 and 4.5 clearly justify combining self-reported survey ratings, open-ended user narratives, and chronometric duration observations so that subjective evaluations of safety, dignity, and care barriers can be interpreted alongside observed temporal patterns of restroom use.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Section 2 Methods (PDF pp. 5-6); Section 4.5 Limitations (PDF pp. 14-15)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: In Section 4 (pp. 10-14), survey results (lower female perceived safety, nappy-changing gaps, support for women's and unisex toilets), qualitative themes (privacy, menstruation, commercial workarounds, care burdens, queues), and chronometric usage observations are woven together to populate the state-municipal-operator accountability framework.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: Integrative interpretation in Sections 4.1 and 4.5 repeatedly relies on 'queuing simulations' and 'objective modeling results' ('while the queuing simulations demonstrate how even modest differences in service time produce disproportionate waiting under peak conditions', p. 10; repeated on p. 15) that are entirely absent from the Methods and Findings sections, and extrapolates untested 40-minute university hallway observations to broader municipal governance claims.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors note cross-strand and literature divergences—including that hygiene complaints appear across men and women qualitatively without a statistically significant quantitative gender gap (Abstract, p. 1; Section 3.1, p. 6; Table 3, p. 9), and the tension between male caregiving difficulties in binary facilities (Table 3, p. 9), formal unisex optimization models, and low male survey support for gender-neutral toilets (Table 2, p. 7; Section 4.2, pp. 11-12).
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Section 3.1 (PDF pp. 6-7); Section 3.2 Table 3 (PDF p. 9); Section 4.2 (PDF pp. 11-12)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: Per MMAT 2018 guidance, overall adherence fails when one or more strands exhibit substantial methodological weaknesses. Here, the quantitative strand suffers from non-representative convenience sampling, low scale reliability (alpha = 0.601), contradictory Likert coding notes, missing inferential statistics for the chronometric study, and references to unpresented queuing simulations, while the qualitative strand omits prompt wording and coding rigor details.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 (PDF pp. 5-6); Sections 3.1-3.3 (PDF pp. 6-10); Sections 4.1 and 4.5 (PDF pp. 10, 14-15)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Glavanits and Fenyes (2026) present an exploratory convergent mixed-methods study embedded within a feminist legal and regulatory analysis of public toilet access in Hungary. Appraised under the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT 2018, combining Qualitative items 1.1-1.5, Quantitative Descriptive items 4.1-4.5, and Mixed Methods items 5.1-5.5), the study demonstrates high methodological concern (weak overall empirical quality, as overall quality in MMAT cannot exceed its weakest component). Strengths include clear exploratory hypotheses (S1-S2), a sound rationale for triangulating self-reported perceptions, open-ended user accounts, and chronometric restroom observations (5.1-5.2), verbatim thematic illustrations (1.4), thoughtful attention to cross-strand nuances regarding unisex acceptability and hygiene (5.4), and accurate doctrinal synthesis of EU/UN equality norms and comparative building codes (Table 1). However, serious empirical limitations affect the quantitative and integrative strands: (1) convenience student and social-media sampling yields a small, non-representative survey sample (N = 97; 72.2% female, 63.9% aged 18-29; response rate unreported; 7 cases omitted in regressions alongside an unexplained 'Hungarian subsample' note) and a single 40-minute campus restroom observation window (N = 56) (4.1, 4.2, 4.4); (2) survey reliability is below conventional thresholds (Cronbach's alpha = 0.601) and Table 2's footnote directly contradicts the main text regarding Likert coding direction, while chronometric timing conflates internal waiting with fixture use and shows conflicting summary means between Table 4 and the text (4.3); (3) Hypothesis H4 is evaluated using raw means without variance or inferential tests, and item-level survey reporting omits non-significant items (4.5); and (4) Sections 4.1 and 4.5 repeatedly invoke 'queuing simulations' as objective modeling evidence despite no simulation methods or results appearing anywhere in the article (5.3, 5.5).
raw_response.overall_rating: High methodological concern (weak empirical quality; constrained by non-representative convenience sampling, low scale reliability and coding contradictions, absence of inferential testing for chronometric observations, and integrative reliance on unreported queuing simulations)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Exploratory convergent mixed-methods primary study (cross-sectional self-administered questionnaire survey N = 97 with open-ended qualitative thematic content analysis n = 30, combined with observational chronometric restroom use duration measurement N = 56) situated within a doctrinal/normative legal analysis
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study design, sampling, and hypotheses H1-H4 in Section 2 Methods (PDF pp. 5-6); quantitative survey sample demographics, reliability, Welch's ANOVAs, OLS regressions, and bootstrap mediation in Section 3.1 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 6-8); qualitative thematic content analysis and verbatim excerpts in Section 3.2 and Table 3 (PDF pp. 8-9); chronometric restroom duration observations in Section 3.3 and Table 4 (PDF pp. 9-10); doctrinal/regulatory framework in Section 1 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 2-5) and integrative legal discussion in Sections 4.1-4.4 (PDF pp. 10-14); methodological limitations in Section 4.5 (PDF pp. 14-15); ethics and consent statements on PDF p. 16.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The article conducts a primary empirical mixed-methods investigation combining quantitative components (a structured cross-sectional survey of N = 97 respondents analyzed via EFA, Welch's ANOVA, OLS regression, and mediation, plus chronometric restroom dwell-time observations of N = 56 users) with a qualitative component (thematic content analysis of open-ended narrative responses from n = 30 respondents in Section 3.2 / Table 3), explicitly triangulating both strands to inform its legal-governance argument. Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool) is the required instrument for genuine mixed-methods primary studies, using Quantitative Descriptive items 4.1-4.5 because the quantitative data describe cross-sectional user perceptions/experiences and observed usage durations without an experimental or quasi-experimental policy/intervention comparator.
